# On a network

Written for: Python developers who build with agentspaces-client.

The client ignores the frame kinds it does not speak and survives every hostile
frame (ROBUSTNESS.md). Every document it reads from the network is in the AgentSpaces
wire encoding: one item under shortest heads, at
most 64 nested levels, definite byte strings and arrays, indefinite maps whose
keys are distinct text, text of shortest-form UTF-8 that is definite up to
3996 UTF-16 units and in Jackson's exact chunks past that, an integer outside
a Java long as a bignum (tag 2 or 3) of at most 1000 bytes, a decimal as a normalized tag 4, a
float64 or a float32 with the one NaN Java writes, and no other tag, simple
value or half float. A bignum decodes to an `int` and a decimal to a
`decimal.Decimal`, and a float32 to a `cbor.Float32`, each of which re-encodes
to the bytes it came from. A protocol record (a frame, a body, a space delta,
a claim, an advertisement, a revocation, a founding, a capability pipe payload) holds exactly the fields
Java's record holds, in its order, each of its kind: no float or text where an
integer belongs, no integer where text or a double belongs, no text where bytes
belong, no tag, an `Instant` and a `Duration` as Java prints them, maps sorted,
and an agent id whose local name holds no `/` and no `:`. It also holds what
Java's record constructor holds: no null where Java requires a value (an
envelope's group, kind, sender, stamp or body; a record's identity, lease or
tags; a lease's holder or kind; a certificate's agent, key, issue instant or
period), a positive dot counter, lease expiry and certificate period, a payload
inline or by reference and never both or neither, an inline payload of at most
64 KiB, and a key epoch of 1 or more when present. A receiver decodes a
carrier only when re-encoding what it decoded gives back exactly the bytes it
received, so a relay cannot relabel a signed frame, and every signature
verifies over the same bytes at every peer. A frame or body that fails counts
in `peer.malformed_frames`, a space delta in `peer.deltas_undecodable`, and
nobody is struck for either. An entry whose payload is outside the encoding
still replicates, and every read skips its value. A stamp is a definite text
item in the canonical `physical:logical:node` grammar: each number `0` or
ASCII digits without a leading zero, a physical that fits a signed 64-bit
integer, a node part present with no colon, no control character and no lone
surrogate. A stamp holds at most 3996 UTF-16 units, so a text in Jackson's chunks is
never a stamp, and `hlc_now` refuses a node past 3965 units. A frame whose stamp is no stamp item does not decode: the peer
drops it before any signature check and counts it in `peer.malformed_frames`.
Every verified frame then passes a `FrameFilter`, which judges the stamp in the order SPEC §9 gives: one
older than five minutes and a sender-and-stamp pair it saw before, then one
past the HLC drift bound by at most five seconds
(`wire.FAR_FUTURE_SKEW_MARGIN_MILLIS`, the room a receiver whose wall runs a
little behind gives an honest peer), one further past it, and one whose
logical counter is above 65536 (`wire.LOGICAL_LIMIT`). It drops each without
a reply and counts it (`peer.frames.stale`, `.replayed`, `.far_future_skewed`,
`.far_future`, `.logical_refused`). Because each stamp has one spelling, the
bytes a signer signed always equal the stamp's re-encoding.

A space delta whose state or claim holds anything but such a stamp (record,
lease, signing or claim stamp) does not decode, as in Java's codec: the peer
drops the whole delta and counts it in `peer.deltas_undecodable` on every
offer. The peer checks a state or claim in this order: its signatures and
certificate, its actor's revocation, then its stamps, so a revoked actor counts
in no stamp counter. It applies `wire.acceptable_hlc` to the record, lease and
signing stamps of a state and to a claim's stamp, and counts a refusal once in
`peer.stamps_logical_refused`. It refuses a state or claim whose record, lease
or claim stamp runs more than an hour past wall + drift + margin and counts it
once in `peer.stamps_far_future_refused`. A state or claim stamped past wall +
drift + margin by less is deferred: it does not merge, it counts once in
`peer.stamps_far_future_deferred`, and it merges when anti-entropy offers it
again after this peer's wall catches up, so an honest taker whose clock a
hostile stamp dragged ahead loses nothing. The peer judges every offer afresh,
so a refused far-future offer merges too once the wall catches up; a memory of
the 4096 most recently offered keys, keyed on the signed content alone, only
keeps each refusal and each deferral at one count. An agent certificate bounds
a record, a claim or an agent-signed state by its validity window alone, so an
agent's record stamp, claim stamp and state `signedAt` meet these same rules.
A state with a null lease stamp decodes and merges nothing, uncounted. A claim
travels as a `TakeClaim` in Java's field order and its signature covers those
bytes; a claim whose fields arrive in another order, or whose epoch, expiry or
bid is null, absent or of another kind, makes its delta undecodable. Bids
order as Java's `Double.compare` orders them, -0.0 below 0.0. As Java's
`mergeClaim` does, the peer drops, uncounted, a claim stamped more than the
drift bound before its entry's issue stamp, and a claim contesting another
holder's claim with a stamp older than the drift bound and Java's 200 ms
settle window. This client offers an empty digest on a pull toward a seed
without `wire.ae=2`, so there it acknowledges no refused state; its partners
re-offer it, and the count stays at one. Toward a seed whose card carries
`wire.ae=2` a pull names a budget of 1 MiB (SPEC annex I.6) and offers this
peer's own text digest of the space, with an `a:<line>` for each verified
state it refused and each revoked holder's claim; when an answer's
`remainder` says states were left out, the peer asks again at once with its
digest, until nothing is left out or an answer changes nothing here. The
digest stays under the 8 MiB frame by keeping the lines a partner would send
first. This client keeps no strikes. `peer.counters()` returns these counts
under the Java node's names (`framesLogicalRefused`, `framesFarFuture`,
`framesFarFutureSkewed`, `stampsLogicalRefused`, `stampsFarFutureRefused`,
`stampsFarFutureDeferred`, `deltasUndecodable`). A ref head reads its advisory
`pdt.issued` and `pdt.issuer` as Java's `Refs` reads them: when the stamp is
absent, null, not text, not acceptable, or past the drift bound plus the
margin, or the issuer is present but null, not text or no agent id, the head
keeps the entry's own stamp and issuer together, and the peer counts nothing.
Every other attribute holds text: a head with a null or non-text value there
does not decode, and the ref counts the entry once in `heads_ignored`, as it
counts a head that breaks a bound or names another kind or ref. A claim on an
entry this replica collected or never held leaves the claim map once its
expiry passes: the peer prunes such claims as a space delta arrives, once the
map holds at least 1024 claims and twice what its last scan left, so the map
stays bounded under churn. Nodes and holders order by UTF-16 code
units, as Java's `String.compareTo` orders them. The local clock clamps a
merged physical one millisecond inside the drift bound, carries a counter past
the limit into the next millisecond, and raises on a node the grammar refuses,
so no stamp it issues repeats, exceeds the limit, breaks the grammar, or runs
past what a receiver admits. The peer counts a kind this client does not speak
in `peer.ignored_kinds` and a body that does not decode in
`peer.malformed_frames`, and the reader goes on. A lost socket is a hiccup: the peer
re-dials the seeds until `close()` (swarm retries, ROBUSTNESS.md §10.3 E5). Each round dials
the seeds in list order, 250 ms apart (RFC 8305), with the seed it lost last, and takes the
first that answers; a refused dial starts the next at once, and a dial that answers after
the winner is closed. Between refused rounds it
waits on the redial table every peer keeps (owner decision 2026-11-23): 5, 10, 20 and 30 s, then 5 s again, each with a random spread
of +/-10%. A link that held for at least 5 s resets the table and is dialled again at once, and a
wake from sleep resets it too: with no link the wake dials at once, and with the link up it
PINGs the seed and drops the link when no answer comes within 2 s (the dead-seed rule), failing over at once however young the link. A
link that ends within `reconnect_interval_s` (5 s, the table's first wait) of its dial
counts as a refused round and waits the table's next step, so a seed that accepts each dial and drops it
at once gets the same pauses (§10.6). A bootstrapped peer reads its beacon again every
`reconnect_window_s` (10 min) with nothing reachable. It then introduces itself again and pulls again what it had pulled
(revocations, advertisements, spaces), counting in `peer.reconnects`; a `take`
in flight keeps polling across the gap. `close()` by the owner is final.
`tests/test_robustness.py` pins each case against a fake seed over TCP, and
`tests/test_tls.py` the tls binding against one over TLS.

## Renewals and the collection horizon (SPEC v0.1.35)

- `peer.renew_entry` renews by the rule of SPEC §7.2. Only the issuer renews,
  the entry must be present and its lease not lapsed here, and the new expiry
  is `max(current, now + extension)`, so a renewal never shortens a lease. A
  renewal the rule leaves unchanged sends nothing and returns `False`; one
  that fails a condition raises `ValueError`. Cancel and write again for a
  shorter lease.
- `Taken.renew` renews the take's claim, as Java's `TakenEntry.renew`: same
  epoch, stamp, holder and bid, a later expiry. It never touches the write
  lease. `Subscription.renew` never shortens a subscription's lease either.
- The peer collects tombstones by SPEC §7.3: a lapsed entry five minutes at
  most after its lapse, a completion two of the space's longest leases after
  its expiry, a withdrawal never before ten minutes (the drift floor). The
  door refuses a collected state a lagging partner offers again and
  acknowledges it for five minutes.
- The peer advertises `wire.horizon=1` (pass `horizon_hint=False` to opt out,
  for one identity run on two nodes). While it and every member of its view
  advertise the hint for three rounds, then one longest lease and five
  minutes more, a withdrawal whose writer it vouches for goes at ten minutes
  past its expiry (`peer.horizon_mode`, `peer.horizon_rule()`).

## Timing, the watchdog and virtual time (SPEC v0.1.36)

- **Answering probes.** A `PING` is answered at once with an `ACK` addressed
  to the prober, and a `PING` that came inside a `RELAY_FRAME` is answered
  back through the seed, as Java answers it. The self-advertisement names the
  seed this peer dialled in `relay.via` (from the TLS handshake on `tls`, from
  the seed's first addressed frame on `tcp`), so every member reaches it
  through that seed. On `tcp` a new link also sends the seed one `PING`, whose
  addressed `ACK` names the seed within one round trip. A changed
  advertisement is issued a millisecond after the one before it, so no
  receiver drops it as a copy.
- **A seed that went silent.** This is the dead-seed rule every dial-only
  client keeps. A link that has carried nothing for 45 s (1.5 times the 30 s
  keepalive bound) is asked with a `PING` to the seed. A link still silent
  when the ping timeout falls due (2 s, the timeout a prober gives each
  `PING`) is dropped and dialled again, the next seed first
  (`peer.links_silent`). Bytes of a frame still arriving count as an answer,
  so a large frame on a slow link is not taken for a dead seed. A seed that
  vanished without closing the socket (power loss, a moved laptop) is so left
  within 47 s of its last frame, and `relay.via` follows the new seed.
- **The seed's anti-entropy round.** The peer answers its seed's `DIGEST`
  (the text round) with one `PULL_RESP`: the states and claims of the spaces
  it holds that the seed's digest does not name (`peer.pulls_answered`). A
  write, renewal, completion or claim of its own that was lost on its only
  link is so repaired at the seed's next round. A state joined from two
  inputs goes as its most advanced signed input, since nobody signed the
  join.
- **A winner's round through the seed.** A `DIGEST` another member addressed
  to this peer and the seed carried is answered only for the spaces where
  this peer holds a displaced claim (a better claim displaced a claim made
  here, whether or not it completed the entry under it, as in the core), with
  only those entries: the displaced claim, and the entry's state where the
  asker lacks it, back through the seed (`peer.displaced_digest_answers`). Each
  asker's answers take a bucket of 16, refilled at 4 a second, so one member
  flooding such rounds cannot starve another's; one held back is counted
  (`peer.relayed_answers_paced`). The seed's own round is never held
  back. Any other `DIGEST` (a relayed one for spaces with nothing displaced,
  or one carrying the fields of the hashed round or of annex I.6, which this
  peer does not advertise) is ignored and counted, as before.
- **Deadlines, not ticks.** The sweep of the spaces waits for the next lapse
  (an entry, a claim, a leased subscription, a collection) or a change, not
  250 ms. Aggregate rounds run every second (Java's `ROUND_PERIOD`) and sleep
  while no epoch is known; `Settle.after("40s", t)` and
  `@on_estimate(settle="PT40S")` take a span, counted in the rounds the
  aggregate runs. An `@on_estimate` that names no rule waits 8 s, as Java's
  `@OnEstimate` does; `settle="0s"` fires on the first estimate. Every round counts toward a settle rule once the epoch was
  heard, so an epoch that went quiet still settles. An estimate unchanged for
  30 s is no longer shared until a share moves it, and one unchanged for an
  hour is forgotten, as in Java. The content swarm's and the PDT
  ticks still run every 250 ms while started. A lost socket ends no loop: the
  sweep, the binder's takes, the aggregate's rounds and those ticks run until
  `close()`.
- **Two clocks.** Stamps and leases another peer reads use wall time; every
  local period uses monotonic time. A wall step moves the subscriptions' leases
  with it, and a forward step past 30 s (a suspend) makes the peer introduce
  itself again, pull again, ask the seed with a `PING` and renew the binder's
  leases at once (`peer.resumes`). A reconnect pausing between rounds when the
  laptop slept dials again at wake, and the redial table starts again. Every
  wall step, a wake's included, judges each take a handler holds at once.
- **A frozen process is a wake too.** A watchdog check that comes back more
  than 30 s late with no wall step (SIGSTOP, a long pause) is treated as the
  wake a suspend is (`peer.late_wakes`): the seed is asked with a `PING`, the
  held takes are judged, and the view pull leaves out the member cards that
  lapsed or are ending, so the seed sends them again. A member whose card ran
  out only while this peer was frozen is asked for, not dropped: until the
  seed's answer, or 11.25 s, it still counts in the horizon's view as lacking
  the hint, the cautious side (`peer.view_reprobes`, as in Ruby and Rust).
- **Late takes.** A take has lapsed when its claim is no longer this peer's (a
  better claim displaced it, or another completed or withdrew the entry, which
  takes the claim with it, as in the core) or its wall-time lease has expired. One that a
  wake found lapsed renews no more, and a result that arrives after the lapse,
  with or without a wake, completes nothing and writes nothing. Each is counted
  once in `bound.late_takes` (`lateTakes` in the core).
- **Counters.** The redial and seed rules count under the names every client
  shares: `peer.seed_pings` (PINGs asking the seed), `peer.wake_pings` (the
  wake's among them), `peer.links_silent`, `peer.resumes`, `peer.seed_dials`
  (dials started) and `peer.late_seed_channels` (connections that answered
  after another seed won, closed). `peer.loop_health()` carries them too, with
  `late_wakes`, `view_reprobes`, `displaced_digest_answers` and
  `relayed_answers_paced`.
- **The watchdog.** One thread per process checks every 2 s that each
  connected peer's reader and sweep live, restarts one that died, and names a
  frame that held the reader past 5 s (`peer.loop_health()`). A watch callback
  runs on the reader, so it should hand long work to a thread.
- **Virtual time.** `Peer(..., time_source=VirtualTime())` drives the same code
  in a test: `advance(seconds)` moves both clocks and wakes every waiter, and
  `step_wall(ms)` moves the wall clock alone (`agentspaces.timesource`).
- **The TTL floor.** The binder warns about a card TTL or a binding's lease
  under 60 s; `Binder(..., ttl_floor=TtlFloor(strict=True))` refuses one
  unless an override names the key and its reason (`agentspaces.ttl`).
- **Displaced claims.** A peer that completed an entry under a claim a better
  claim later displaced offers its claim again (at once, then after 1, 2, 4, 8
  and 16 s, six offers at most), so the winner can pair it with the completion
  and not do the work again (SPEC §7.4). The backoff is judged on the
  monotonic clock, so a wall step neither fires the offers at once nor holds
  them back.
